utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Please be seated. And may we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Ruth Karper. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Branko Lukic assisted by Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And before we start today first a remark, a special gratitude has to be expressed in the direction of the booth because I'm aware of the problem it causes when we come with numerous documents and ask them to be not translated, I wouldn't put it this way, but have an interpretation that grants access to all the Judges at the same time. And I can only assure all participants here that it will be a limited number of times where we need such an exercise. But we have to live with three languages, and sometimes it's important to have access for all the parties at the same time. Once again, thank you all for this special effort. I heard that there would be a motion by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. At this time the Defence would like to make an application and a motion which is similar to the motion that was raised orally last Thursday at the end of the testimony of the witness, which in essence seeks to bar, prohibit, and to limit the testimony particularly of this next individual witness who I believe is not -- does not have a pseudonym, so I think we can identify his name, Mr. Mevludin Sejmenovic. Specifically we raise this issue out of grave concern because yesterday we were given a statement purportedly signed by the witness on June 11th, 2002, yesterday. That statement in and of itself is inconsistent with the four prior statements offered by this witness in three specific trials and one written statement offered previously to us in the year 2000. Our motion in essence seeks to have the Court limit the OTP from utilising fact witnesses as opinion witnesses. We believe that this is a violation of the Rules of Procedure and Disclosure. We believe it's a violation of the current decisional authority here before the ICTY. It's certainly as violation of the rights offered to protect the accused in this case, and it's a violation of the equality of arms as previously identified by this Chamber as well as other courts. Specifically, for the record to note, that on May 28th, 2001, when this witness testified in a separate proceeding identified as OTP versus Sikirica, he was asked questions about Dr. Stakic, what posts he held, and what were the position of those posts. He answer ad page 3982, specifically lines 9 through 11, that he had no knowledge of what post Dr. Stakic held at the time or what his involvement was at the time as of May 25th, and then he corrects himself and says May 24th, 1992. If we compare that testimony with what the Prosecutor has done while interviewing this witness and preparing him to testify, we can see that the witness now has reviewed a significant number of documents, has prepared himself to give opinion testimony, not fact testimony, but opinion testimony as it relates to this particular accused and defendant Dr. Stakic. Specifically Rule 94 bis states and mandates, doesn't just offer it as a professional, but mandates that if the OTP is required or wants to call a witness as an opinion witness, they must give us 21 days' notice of what that opinion testimony will be, not less than 24 hours as is the case yesterday by offering us that statement. Secondly, it mandates that they tell us what is the basis of that opinion, i.e., specifically what are the documents that that witness relied upon, what are the documents that that witness reviewed, and what videotapes he reviewed which he sets forth in his statement that he reviewed videotapes. This, Your Honour, in our opinion is a gross breach of the rules before this Tribunal and it is an attempt to not allow a fair trial to proceed here before the Court. We believe that the Court should bar and limit the testimony of Mr. Sejmenovic to that on his four prior offers of proof and testimony that he has provided. Simply stating we expect him and expected him to give fact testimony as it relates to his involvement in Prijedor through Trnopolje as well as perhaps the conversation that he had subsequent in late August, early September, 1992, where he purports that he saw Dr. Stakic at a certain event. We don't have an objection to that. We do have an objection to his opinion testimony as is outlined and as is specifically set forth in his June 11th 2000 witness statement. We have also prepared, if I may or if the Court would allow the Registrar, an application in written form generally allowing or generally asking this Court to stop the practice by the Prosecutor of asking fact witnesses opinion testimony which is beyond that which they have previously disclosed to us. We have not filed it with the Registrar. We expect to do so at the first break or soon thereafter, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May it for clarification nevertheless be distributed immediately that we know what you are aiming at directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, could the usher please distribute the document. I have the impression before accepting the observations by the OTP it's the first time ever that I had the chance to hear a pre-examination before the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, but of course no doubt we've got your point. But please, the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Sejmenovic, first of all, can I deal with what's called "late disclosure" of the extra statement. In fact, like all witnesses, as Mr. Ostojic is aware, the witness was what's called proofed, and I know Your Honours are all aware of that, that is to say because it's a long time since he has reviewed his testimony. He was shown a number of documents during the course of the proofing, and he was asked a number of further questions with specific reference to the case against Stakic. Before that, the other cases in which he has testified with that one exception that Mr. Ostojic has referred to, because Stakic was not the subject of the proceedings, he wasn't asked any particular questions. On this occasion, because the information that he was giving was new in normal circumstances the Defence would merely be provided with an outline of anything else he was going to testify to. But on this occasion, because it was new or could be described as new information, it was thought right that he should put this into the form of a signed statement. That was only given to the Defence yesterday. However, the note that was taken during the proofing by the investigator was actually supplied to the Defence, I think, on Friday, at least I hope it was. There was a rough note, or it should have been. Your Honour, however, that's not the point. Mr. Sejmenovic is without a shadow of a doubt the most best -- I'm sorry, that's not good English. The best-placed witness to assist this Tribunal on some of the documents that Your Honours are going to be asked to consider because he was, first of all, a member of the Bosnia-Herzegovina assembly until 1992, was in the area throughout most of the events up until July of 1992, and therefore can assist Your Honours not as an expert, but as someone through his role in the political life, both in Prijedor itself and at the higher levels, with a possible interpretation of those documents. Your Honour, as far as the difference between what he said in his testimony in the Sikirica case and what he said in this statement, Your Honours, of course the first question that I should be asking about is is this information you knew at the time or is it information that you've gleaned from your examination of the documents and the evidence that he gives, if the answer is through examination of the documents, well then, Your Honours, we will treat it with -- we'll give it the weight that it deserves. If there is an answer that he knew it at the time, then he of course can be cross-examined on what he said on an earlier occasion. The idea is that Your Honour should look at the evidence in this case with the best assistance you can receive from any witness whose in a position to do so. Your Honours are here to ascertain, as far as is possible, what is the truth of what happened in 1992 in Prijedor. And so we submit we're not putting forward this man as an expert in the sense of Rule 94; we're putting him forward as someone who has knowledge, empirical knowledge of the events and can assist Your Honours in how to deal with the documents. May I say I was taken a bit by surprise this morning because I wasn't aware that was going to be raised, and if Your Honour wants a fuller submission and possibly authority quoted, then I'd have to ask for time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt as regards the witness before us, notwithstanding the need to decide on this more general submission we just got, wouldn't it be fair if we accept vice versa a mutual presumption of fairness, saying that in this case the OTP will act, taking into account your comments, and of course it is for you to object on a case-by-case basis. I wonder whether it's possible to have a general rule, especially to have a general rule when we -- especially also the Judges overstepped on purpose sometimes asking questions on opinion, knowing very well about the limited probative value of this, and sometimes the outcome of such questions were, put it this way, not always to the disadvantage of the Defence. So therefore, I think the threshold is a little bit different one to an ordinary criminal court. When it, in our case before us, we come to the point and to the question, for example, I didn't -- I'm not aware of this, what you said, the witness has changed or suddenly has enhanced knowledge, then it's, of course, for the cross-examination to find out, or in the meantime, when it's a real question of an opinion, and here it's not to find out as it was with other witnesses appearing for the first time, you give them a chance to express their feelings, so there is a slight difference. When there's a question you regard in more or less opinion and not fact based, then please feel free to object. But I don't want to conclude without saying that the working method indeed has to be changed a little bit. We were confronted yesterday by a deluge of first of all exhibit lists with two entire files, and normally I'm, as a judge, as a presiding judge, I want to read everything, and it was not possible for me to read everything in advance. And then in addition, receiving the transcripts of some hundred pages of three former cases. It is impossible. We all have to take care, and I mentioned it several times, that we do not die in too much information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say first of all, I'm sorry about the, as you put it, the deluge of documents. I understand that the list was provided to Your Honours' staff on Monday. Your Honour, I appreciate that, that it is a deluge, and the fault is entirely mine because of the other commitments I've had, and I think Your Honour -- I want to come back to the problem I have later on. I was unable to too far in advance to prepare a list for Your Honours. Equally, the witness himself, because of the expense of bringing witnesses over, was not able to go through the documents until quite recently. But Your Honour, I do apologise. As for the transcripts, again, Your Honour, I understand that the list was available. I wasn't aware -- the practice is that the transcripts would be given -- are really only provided for the Defence for the purposes of inconsistent testimony. But I understand that Your Honours are anxious to have them in advance. So what I can say, Your Honours, I'm sorry about that. I'm afraid it is my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for these comments

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may briefly, Your Honour, respond to the Court's comments and reply to the response earlier, previously given by the OTP and Ms. Joanna Korner, what's critical we believe is that it's not just the testimony that this witness gave in the Sikirica case. This witness was identified as a fact witness in an identical indictment which involved a co-accused in 1998, Dr. Kovacevic, the late Dr. Kovacevic. His testimony, and those counts in that indictment against Dr. Kovacevic parallel and are similar to those against our client here today Dr. Stakic. At that point, this witness was not asked to give and refused, in fact - and Ms. Korner can verify that - to give opinion testimony and merely was called as a fact witness. Now he's being offered late in the case, and we suggest that this is clearly trial by ambush, that they are bringing a witness in, although three weeks before he was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sitting here with the Office of the Prosecutor, then sent home, then returned, and on the eve of his testimony, we get his written statement which purports now to have opinions of certain relationships between either the Crisis Staff and the military and the police, et cetera. We think it's vital, and we again do not object to his testimony from a fact witness perspective or to share with us his experience at the republic level which he may or may not have had during that time period. But we object to him giving specific opinion testimony relating to counts in the complaint as it relates to Dr. Stakic. That's a clear violation of the Rules, both the spirit and the letter of all the Rules within this Tribunal, and all the decisional authority here. So again, we must reiterate that it's not something that is new to the Office of the Prosecutor since it is a witness that they had offered as a witness on three prior occasions, taken his statement on this fourth occasion, and now are calling him for a fifth time s it relates to Dr. Stakic. So I just wanted to make the record clear as to specify with respect to this witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these comments. And before I give the floor to the OTP, just one additional remark: We should refrain from pleading before hearing the case, and we would -- we should refrain from commenting on a witness statement before the Judges had the chance to hear the statement. Of course, including all the Rules, all the possibilities for the Defence to point out if they so believe that it's more or less a cut and paste from another interview. We had these problems already in the past with another witness, and I believe it was impressive for the Judges the way it was pointed out by the Defence that some sentences were found nearly identical in a statement "against" Dr. Kovacevic. And now, in the case before us. Therefore, I think we shouldn't go into further details. Please don't hesitate to object if you regard it necessary, and we will make our rulings. I think we should start immediately with the witness and not to waste -- sorry, the word waste is to that extent wrong, because it's indeed helpful that the Defence pointed out before what is at stake with the witness before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I very briefly, just before the witness comes in, deal with a problem that is entirely mine, but is a result of what happened last week in the Brdjanin/Talic case. We were delayed for a number of reasons, and therefore the witness that I was due to call did not begin testifying until the middle of Friday afternoon. As a result, he has not finished his evidence in chief. Now, although I can get another counsel to take over when cross-examination starts, and indeed for re-examination, I cannot ask another counsel to take over with the witness in chief. Your Honour, it's likely, particularly if there's going to be objections raised which Your Honours will have to rule on that Mr. Sejmenovic will not complete his testimony in chief by Friday. I will therefore be in the position that on Monday afternoon because both cases at the moment are sitting on Monday afternoon where I am part heard with a witness in this Chamber and part heard with a witness in the other Chamber. Your Honour, I would make the application, if I could to Judge Agius's court to sit in the morning instead, to try and do a swap, but no counsel from that case are in this country and I know that Mr. Ackerman is not returning from the States until Monday lunchtime. I understand Mr. Koumjian raised this yesterday with Your Honours. I know that it's possible with the agreement of the other case to do an alternate for, say, one morning. But if Your Honours feel that's not possible, then all I can ask Your Honours to do is perhaps -- I understand that you're all in the process of reading various documents into the record for the purposes of translation. It is for that to happen on Monday afternoon whilst I complete the evidence in chief of the witness in the Brdjanin/Talic case, which I estimate will be finished by the first break in the afternoon. And then for me to return to that court to pick up examination-in-chief. Your Honour, the most desirable would be if Your Honours could sit on the morning on Monday, but I understand that's maybe not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, but you were absent yesterday, and probably not sufficiently informed by Mr. Koumjian. It was quite clear what I said. For unfortunate reasons, since weeks, I tried to have a courtroom for this Friday in exchange to Monday because it's impossible for me to be here on Monday morning. So therefore, there is no place, there's no room for hearing on Monday morning. We have to continue on Monday morning, and we have to continue as scheduled. Hopefully, we can finalise the witness until tomorrow in the evening. Otherwise, we should find a way with the help of the Registry. Nevertheless -- I don't know if the other participants are available on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then also this attempt doesn't work. Then we have to proceed. And in principle, please understand, but in principle, we have to accept the OTP as one OTP. And the internal organisation is, first of all, not a problem of the Bench. As of courtesy, of course, we will try our best. Please, let's start. Probably we'll come through until tomorrow in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've made the position clear. Can I say this: Of course, the OTP acts as one institution. It's unusual, may I say, for two cases to be conducted like this, and it's most unusual for this position to arise because normally there are sufficient lawyers. But it has unfortunately arisen so all I can do, and I understand Your Honour, we can review the position tomorrow and, if necessary, that Your Honours may take something else early on in the afternoon on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. So let us please hear the witness right away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now I can hear the interpretation from English into Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And may we immediately turn to the examination-in-chief, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher could lower the ELMO for the moment because it's actually interrupting the line of sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, is your name Mevludin Sejmenovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born on the 15th of October, 1962?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you a Bosniak by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a Bosniak by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think that you've spent most of your life, or spent up until 1992 most of your life in Prijedor, on the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by 1992, were you living in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was living in Trnopolje at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1992, were you a married man?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. In 1992, I was not married.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to deal briefly, please, with your background until 1990. I think you completed primary education in Kozarac, and then secondary education in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you did your military service, did you serve in an artillery unit?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I served in an artillery unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after doing that, did you go to university, and then go to study mining in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to come next to the 1990 elections, the first multiparty elections. Did you join one of the parties?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I participated in one of the initiatives to establish a political parties. Before political parties were established, I decided to take part in the organising of the SDA. And I was a member of the steering or initiative committee of the SDA which was later registered as a normal political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the election campaign in 1990, were you elected the first president of the SDA in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I was elected the first vice-president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. My fault. And during the elections, did you win a seat in the assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in the Chamber of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the chamber of municipalities at the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to have a look, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, this was an exhibit that was not part of the Rule 65 ter ones. It is a copy of the gazette showing the results of the 1990 elections. And I think Your Honours already have been given that, or should have been. I think all the witness needs is the copy in the Bosnian language. If Your Honours go first of all to page 4 of the English translation, and if the witness could look at I think it's on the second -- it's the page in the original is 1243. Now, it's the third section of this document, Mr. Sejmenovic, which is headed "Deputies elected in the constituencies by lists of candidates." And we see "the Banja Luka constituency." I think the witness may not have the right document. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have been given a different document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. We'll just check. It should be the -- the Bosnian version should look like this. All right. Can I hand mine in. Yes, we'll hand one in for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the registry please help out. I'm not aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the last document in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We got numerous bundles of in preparation of today. Probably there are some over there. I can't see anything looking like that what you just indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the -- at least my copy of the Bosnian version looks like. The English version looks like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. Not available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're handing up some more copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we also, although it's within the Witness Number 45 potential exhibits, we see what seems to be a reference to it, but we don't seem to have it in our documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You do. I'm told you do have them. It's the last document in a bundle provided by Ms. Karper, put in your lockers last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We went through it. We looked at that, and the minutes are the last -- minutes of a meeting are the last bundle within that. But we'll look again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm only going to refer to two pages. Perhaps we put the English translation on the ELMO. That will assist everyone. Usher, could we put on to the ELMO out of the English version, please, page 4. The bottom portion under --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Bottom portion, Roman numeral III.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I'm sorry about that. Now, if we look at that, we can see it's headed "Deputies elected in the constituencies by lists of candidates, Banja Luka constituency." And we can see that under the list of the SDA from Sarajevo there is a Dr. Mujadzic. There's a misspelling, I think, in the English translation of his name. Were these deputies elected to the chamber of -- it was different from the chamber -- I've Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. forgotten what it's called now I'm afraid. They were elected to which? Citizens chamber, I think.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: These deputies, yes, were elected to the chamber of citizens in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina in one of the two existing chambers within the parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And now I'm going to ask you, please, Mr. Sejmenovic, if you can turn in your document to page 1257, and we'll put up on the ELMO page 39 of the translation. And do we see there the record of the constituency of the municipality of Prijedor, and do we see in that that you were elected with just over 50 per cent of the vote?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Marko Pavic was a another candidate who seemed to be a candidate for a number of people. There was no candidate there for the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The SDS party did not have a candidate for this Chamber, at least, in the Prijedor municipality, and they decided to support Marko Pavic, who was a candidate of the coalition of left-wing parties which were descendants of the former League of Communists. This was never made public as a formal position of the party. However, the fact remains that the party did not offer its candidate for this seat. And the fact that Marko Pavic received this number of votes proves that the SDS had chosen him as their candidate. And in the first round, nobody won the necessary 51 per cent. That was the reason why we had a second round. And I won a sufficient number of votes during that second round and received a seat in the republic parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, looking at that -- at this document, we can see that for the chamber of citizens, there were a list of a number of people who were elected. For the chamber of municipalities, does it appear there was only one representative per municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the election system in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Wider constituency existed for the chamber of citizens. They were organised on a regional principle. There were lists of candidates, party lists of candidates, and each party offered a number of their candidates on each list by circling the name of one of the candidates. Regardless of the order on the list, the first several candidates according to the number of votes were made members of this chamber, unlike the chamber of citizens, the chamber of municipalities adopted the immediate system of voting, the direct system of voting. Candidates were chosen according to that system. The chamber of municipalities was supposed to represent equally the interests of all municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that's why each municipality offered one deputy to that chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You can put the document away now, and we can take it off the ELMO. Now, in Prijedor itself, in the municipal elections to the assembly, was it the SDA who took the highest number of votes?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the SDA who received the highest number of seats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think the SDS followed close behind. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had been elected a member of the republican-level assembly. Did that give you any rights to attend the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had that right, and I fully exercised it. I attended the sessions of the Municipal Assembly, and I also had the right to attend the sessions of the municipal government and some of the municipal bodies. My main function was to observe problems at the local level and receive any complaints and comments to that effect, and to convey that to the republican-level assembly. So by virtue of my mandate, I had the obligation to follow the events taking place at the level of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to deal first --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: And at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to deal first in your testimony with the events at the republic level of the assemblies you attended and what was happening. Just briefly, after the 1990 elections, was there any kind of change in the atmosphere of the -- at the level of the republic assembly.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Major changes occurred. Compared to the atmosphere which reigned before the elections and at the time of the agreements on the possible coalitions, prior to the elections, the main focus of our party, and this is something that we heard from other political parties as well, was to defeat the communists. That was the main objective of our political party, and we had full support to that effect. And we endeavoured to take part in the process that had already started in eastern Europe. However, immediately after the elections we were faced with the situation in which the SDS had completely different plans. They were not satisfied with simply defeating the communists. They started expressing certain aspirations which threatened to disrupt the relations with other political parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were those aspirations that they were expressing in public?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Publicly, they expressed full and absolute support for the Yugoslav People's Army, which had already violated federal laws. Also, publicly, they spoke about the fact that the Serb population was threatened, so regardless of the results of the elections and regardless of the fact that they had adequate number of representatives within the parliament, they were trying to further this argument that they had at the time at various political meetings and sessions. They made comparisons with the situation in Croatia with what was happening to the Serb population in that republic. And finally their only mission, at least that's how it seemed to be in the parliament, was to represent the interests of Yugoslavia and not Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In June of 1991, the war with Croatia broke out. Did that have an effect on the, as it was, the governing structures?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: When the war actually broke out in Croatia, when the former JNA started military activities in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, a rift occurred between the SDA and SDS and between the SDS and all other political parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The SDA expressed absolute support for the war in Croatia. They appealed to the volunteers to go and fight in the Republic of Croatia, and that was made public. However, the official position of the relevant institutions and authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was opposite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say it was opposite, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: All political parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the exception of the SDS and the Serb radical party were against the JNA killing people in the Republic of Croatia. Up until that time, this was an army in whose establishment and functioning, all republics of the former Yugoslavia participated. However at one point in time, the former JNA started making moves which fell outside its legal framework. They attacked Slovenia, and then continued with an open war against Croatia. This war was preceded by certain political actions in which Serb population in the Republic of Croatia was mobilised. The Yugoslav People's Army formally appeared on the scene as a savior of the Serb population in the Republic of Croatia. Obviously they -- at that time, they started taking actions in the territories which had nothing to do with the Serb population in Croatia. They set up a number of blockades and various forms of obstructions. At the same time, there were quite a few soldiers, quite a few volunteers from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who went to Croatia and took part in these military operations. So there was a major disagreement concerning a very important political issue. We had reasonable explanations and arguments to support our position. We had law on our side. But on the other side, the other side was mighty. This situation made it impossible to reach an agreement within the parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in respect of mobilisation for the purposes of fighting in Croatia, what was the attitude expressed by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The attitude of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was as follows: Their position was that they could not prevent people to volunteer into the JNA and to respond to their mobilisation orders. However, they also made it clear that they were against that war. They considered it to be illegal, and they did not recommend that. So the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not explicitly prohibit individuals from exercising that right. Those who received callup papers were free to join because had they forbidden this, they would have entered into an open conflict with the JNA and they would have made it possible for the JNA to start attacking certain parts and areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was like walking on a razor's edge. You could fall on both sides at any moment. So that was a kind of compromise at the moment. The JNA constituted a force which could not be prevented. We had our official position, but it also included the possibility of letting the volunteers, mainly Serb volunteers, to join. We simply felt that we were not able to openly confront those people who had already been indoctrinated to that effect. So it was left up to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal with you with the events of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I just heard somebody speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I want to deal with the events that took place within the assembly itself in September, October 1991 in the republic. But before that, was there a policy that was discussed by the SDS of what was called "regionalisation"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, there was such a thing. And long before the bloody events that were to follow. In mid-1991, even in the first half of 1991, the SDS came forward with proposals to carry out regionalisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, allegedly for economic reasons and solely for economic reasons, new regions were to be established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- I'm going to ask you the reasoning behind it. But was one of those regions what became known as the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that include within its geographical boundaries the Municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. However, I must provide an additional explanation. Even before the elections, four decades before the elections, this economic regionalisation had already been in place. There was a community formally called the "Association of Municipalities of Banja Luka." And the "Association of Municipalities of Bihac." These communities were set up, were put together, based on mutual interests, traffic interests, transport interests, economic interests. This was always there. And after the SDS started the initiative in the parliament, we tried to explain this to them and we requested from them an explanation. We wanted them to explain why the existing regional division was not good enough, but they failed to provide one. Perhaps two or three months later, they started to speak openly about were they actually employed by economic regionalisation which is how they had referred to it earlier. Of course, we knew very well what they were talking about because we had the same sort of process in Croatia, which had taken very much the same course. And independent regions had been established which practically seceded from Croatia, according to the same plan, the same model. In Croatia, it was also done by the Serbian Democratic Party founded by Jovan Raskovic the psychologist. First, they demanded economic regionalisation, then they established regions, then they cut off communications with other areas of Croatia, then they proclaimed autonomy, and then at last the JNA arrived and secured so to speak these regions. We saw this on TV. We saw this through the media and learned from people who knew what was going on. We realised that the same plan was about to be implemented in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The only thing we had to our advantage against this idea is the existent regional -- economic regionalisation, and we were ready to embark on a new model, but we wanted it to be rational, done according to real economic standards. Very soon, however, it turned out that all that was really at stake was the SDS's ambition to set up new regions, but such regions as were sometimes not even inhabited by Serbs, including municipalities or parts of municipal areas that were mixed in terms of population. We realised immediately that this could lead to the same consequences as it did in Croatia, and we opposed this for as long as we could by political means. Once we were no longer able to oppose, the SDS just simply independently proclaimed the Autonomous Region in Herzegovina and in Banja Luka and started to establish organs of state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the discussions that took place at the republic level assembly, who were the most vocal in favour of this plan of regionalisation from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, who comes from Banja Luka. The idea was to round Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Banja Luka off as an economic region. He discussed this idea several times, so there were discussions in parliament. He used to bring maps and explain the demographic and economic arguments and applied other criteria, too. But it was his task to get this idea implemented in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, come September of 1991, what happened as far as -- later SDS participation in the assembly was concerned?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In late 1991, the SDS started with increasing frequency to give ultimatums in the parliament. So they said: "Either you'll go along with this, or this assembly will cease to be legitimate and legal." So this culminated in late 1991 and early 1992 when the Serb delegates, that's the SDS, and radical party delegates, walked out of the parliament. They occupied a room in the parliament that was free and proclaimed this to be the Serbian Assembly. In the opposition, there were other ethnic groups. Other ethnic groups were represented, and those who remained in the parliament continued to function. But from that moment on, they were the only legitimate assembly of the Serbian people. And what remained of the former parliament as they said was maybe an assembly of the Croat and Muslim people, but certainly not fully representing Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was their view. What they did was not based in any way on law, on -- it had no constitutional basis. But they still went through with it. So the situation was as it was. Regardless of that, the parliament could still function according to the constitution because it had the sufficient number of representatives of all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in September of 1991, did you become aware of the, as it were, declaration of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did hear about the proclamation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. It was public. It was publicly proclaimed. And it was clear to all those would followed parliamentary sessions that what was taking place now is what we had warned about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to have a look, please, at the statute of the so-called Autonomous Region of Krajina which was 65 ter number 26, Your Honours. It's in the binder, second document. And I'd like the witness to be given the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry I forgot to ask for the last document to be made a court exhibit. Could that be made S131, that is, the gazette for the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then admitted as under this number as usual A in English, B, B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if everybody has got a copy, we needn't put it up on the ELMO. First of all, had there been before this so-called declaration, ever been a regional assembly like this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. We can't proceed this way. We are confronted with a deluge as I said, four or five binders of documents, and we can't find them immediately. Please proceed in a way that we can see it on the video. It's not a guessing game, and we don't want to go into this exercise and run through our binders here and there. Please present it in another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I had understood that Your Honours had all got the documents given to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have it, but we don't have a finding tool where in which binder it is. It's five binders you present for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. At the break we'll see what else we can do for finding this for you. Can we put up, please, on the ELMO the first page of the English translation. And we can see at the top, if you just put it down slightly, usher, so we can see, it's the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and then statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And could you pull up the bottom so we can see the date on it. Banja Luka, September 1991. Now, could we put up the second page. Can we look at Article 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The Autonomous Region of Krajina is the association of the following municipalities," and there follows a list of municipalities which "have united on the basis of voluntariness, solidarity and equality and for the purpose of effecting long-term cooperation, coordination of development plans and realising of other common interests.' The municipalities there, Mr. Sejmenovic, do not include Prijedor, as we can see. Was there a common characteristic between the ones that are listed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. They shared the same communications, roads. They are in the Una/Sana River valley, between Vrbas Banja Luka all the way to Bosanska Dubica and Bosanski Novi. This is the same area, one and the same area, including Sanski Most. Of course, neither Sanski Most nor Prijedor have been included, as far as I can tell from this list. Excuse me. Earlier, both Prijedor and Sanski Most used to belong to the same association of municipalities. That was before the war, so to the same economic region. But they are not on this list. Why? Well, that's perhaps a question to be asked of those who set up this economic region. Prijedor and Sanski Most were later made to join the region by force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Prijedor and Sanski Most, was there a majority of Serbs contained within the populous there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was not predominantly Serb. In Prijedor and Sanski Most, Muslim, Bosniak, and Croat people were the predominant population. And other ethnic groups also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, next at Article 3 which states that "The peoples of the Autonomous Region of Krajina shall decide on matters within the jurisdiction of the ARK through their elected representatives in the assembly of the Autonomous Region, the assembly of the republic, and the assembly of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, or through a referendum." First, I go back to the question I started to ask you. Had there been such a regional assembly before the establishment of this one?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Its name was different, but it did exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was it called?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Association of municipalities of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that the -- before that association which you say was the forerunner of this assembly, had there been such an assembly, whatever you'd like to call it, in place at a regional level?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the period before this statute and this region?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the association of the municipalities of Banja Luka came into existence, which was we know in April of 1991, had there been any such assembly with representatives of the various municipalities appearing at a regional assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Not in this shape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if we just briefly have a look at a couple more of the articles. Could we look at Article 10, please, which states that "other municipalities may join the Autonomous Region of Krajina. A municipality wishing to join shall submit a request to do so to the assembly of the Autonomous Region..." And then various other regulations. Now, you've told us a moment ago that Prijedor and Sanski Most were forced into joining this region. Did Prijedor ever, until after April 1992, send representatives -- or the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, I should say, to this assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. Prijedor was annexed by force by -- through the use of weapons. Representatives of the legal government were killed. There was a coup, and following that, Prijedor was annexed by the Autonomous Region of Krajina and its already-existing institutions. As far as concerns the Prijedor Municipal Assembly and the municipal government, as long as it was functioning properly, a request like that was never sent to Banja Luka. There could be no consensus because it was clear what sort of a region was coming into existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, can we look just at Article 16 which states that "the Autonomous Region of Krajina shall monitor the situation and coordinate activities for the organisation and implementation of preparations for all people's defence in accordance with the law, municipal defence plans, and the republic defence plan." Now, who legally in Prijedor, under the Bosnia-Herzegovina constitution was responsible for the defence of each -- in each municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In the municipalities, if a need should arise, the Territorial Defence was in charge of defending the municipality, as well as the existing police forces. Also, the reserve police forces. The military, if any, the reserve component in the area. In a socialist system, this was really well organised and well regulated. All the different levels of national defence were fully elaborated and detailed in the former system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, was there any provision for a body such as this one to coordinate activities for the organisation and implementation of preparations?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. Not this sort of body, and not organised in this way. It never had anything to do with defence. So regional level had nothing to do with national defence level. This was at the republic level, at the municipal level, and at the local self-government level, or from the army point of view, according to parameters the army used to organise their territories. But as far as the regional centres are concerned, this sort of thing had never been organised through associations of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effect did this particular body, the assembly of the Autonomous Region have practically on what happened in the Prijedor region after it was set up?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We can talk about the period preceding the coup in Prijedor, that is, before the takeover. And then the period after the takeover. Which period do you want me to speak about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the moment, very briefly, just the period before the takeover. Did this assembly have any practical authority over events or bodies in the Prijedor region?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Not in the Prijedor region. Whatever authority it could exercise was through SDS people who took part in the work of the municipal government and municipal organs. But not in any other legal way, as Prijedor was still a legal and legitimate community which means that the legally elected government was in place with all its functions. There were obstacles to its work, but it did continue to function. As far as the effect on the population was concerned, that was a major issue. The Autonomous Region of Krajina at the moment of its founding took over the military and television repeaters and installations on Mount Kozara. And they interrupted the radio and TV programmes. They started to show TV Belgrade programmes for the whole day. It made it possible for the military to show military programmes all the time about the sufferings of Serbs in Croatia, history programmes about the sufferings of Serbs in World War II. So this had a huge effect on the Serbian population, a mobilising effect so to speak. And at the same time, it intimidated the other ethnic groups because they were not represented in these programmes, especially not in any affirmative sense. So this was a stage of intense propaganda which continued until the takeover.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure whether this document has already been exhibited, the ARK statute. We're just checking. I don't think it has. Your Honours, may I ask for the admission of this as S132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do object, Your Honour, based on relevance and also based on the testimony provided by the witness who clearly states that as of September 1991, Prijedor was not, at least pursuant to the article that he referenced, was not a party of the ARK. So we object to that. In addition, the witness clearly testified that no members of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly were invited or asked to participate in any assembly meetings from the Autonomous Region of Krajina. So on those three grounds, we object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, do I have a right to reply to that objection?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence under the given number, A in English; B in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm told Your Honour Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 1

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. First of all, my apologies for the delay. The rule says that justicia should act blindfolded, but what is a judge without glasses. So therefore, please understand. In addition, coming back to the documents, is it correct that some of the documents you're presenting today are available both in English and in French?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't do anything about it this week because the counsel in the Brdjanin/Talic case are not here. But it may well be that they themselves had it translated in the Brdjanin/Talic case, counsel for General Talic, had some of these documents translated into French. I'm going to make an inquiry on Monday and ask if they can be supplied to this Chamber where there are common documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would indeed assist our work enormously, and therefore I'm grateful. And I'm looking forward to the end of the examination of this witness. Nevertheless, if there are, as you did already in the beginning, if there are any crucial points in a document you believe are especially valid, please let the witness read it out. And please understand, Witness, that we have to work in this way that we have access to the content of all documents for all participants at the same time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just so that I understand, if there's a document where a section is important, Mr. Sejmenovic should read it in the original, and it will then be translated, rather than me reading the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I want to move to a different but allied point. You were the vice-president of the SDA board in Prijedor, you told us earlier.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a main board of the SDA situated in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from time to time, would you receive instructions from the main board?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your obligation as a municipal board to put those instructions into effect?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the SDA ever issue instructions, the main board, I'm sorry, to you in the municipal board in Prijedor in respect of matters to do with defence or the ordering of matters which lay within the competence of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the orders or instructions concerning the defence are concerned, the SDA was active in preparing such decisions at the level of the party. These decisions were then implemented through the state institutions. Practically speaking, it meant that at the local level, we would spot a problem, or at the level of the republic. Then the party bodies at the level of the republic would discuss the issue, would discuss the problem, clubs of MPs at the parliament would discuss, then we would adopt a common position problem which we would then expose to the parliament or -- and make an adequate request to the government to implement such conclusions. We never received any specific orders or instructions which we would be required to implement outside this framework, outside the adequate government bodies. We participated at all levels of the government. One thing is sure, we could never violate party instructions concerning the overall policy of the party, nor could we change the decisions which had been adopted by the parliament and other state organs. As far as the field work is concerned, we merely assisted in the implementation of the decisions that had been reached at the level of the relevant institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just before we broke, we were having a look at the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the article which dealt with defence. I would like you now, please, to have a look --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if Your Honours could look in the bundles which I hope you have for a document which is marked with the number Rule 65 ter, number 24 and it is a document dated the 11th of September, 1991. It should be the very first one in the... just so that we can all see it, if we could put the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is headed "The Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, president." Dated "Sarajevo, the 11th of September, 1991." And then "Instructions for all municipal boards of the Serbian democratic party of BiH." And it's signed at the bottom and stamped Radovan Karadzic, president of the SDS. Mr. Sejmenovic, could you just read, please, in the original language the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: "President of the Serb democratic party is issuing the following instruction to its municipal boards." I quote: "In view of information which we have become aware and which concerns the planning of commando actions in order to incapacitate the roads in Bosnia-Herzegovina, please make sure to provide round-the-clock guards at all bridges located in your area."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then could you read the third paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: "This task is of utmost importance and must be considered a priority matter and carried out in full and unconditionally. It should be implemented in cooperation with organs of the authorities in such a manner that you improve the safety of travel and do not create chaos by setting up roadblocks or intercepting traffic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now had you received any instruction like this ever from the main board of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This appears to be an instruction to the municipal boards of the SDS to set up guards at various roads. Was this, in your view, a matter that ought to be dealt with on a political party level?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was not. This is an issue which cannot be dealt by political parties, if they are functioning appropriately. These matters concern the police. They are within the exclusive competence of the police. If such a problem is spotted at the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then it is the Minister of the Interior who should issue an order to this effect to the local police stations so that they mobilise their personnel and comply with the request. This is dated the 11th of September, 1991, when the overall state system was functioning adequately, including the police and other relevant structures. So it is unclear why such orders or instructions had to be put into effect in a parallel way. In this document, the president of a political party is taking up the position and the capacity of the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask that this be admitted as S133. I should tell Your Honours it was a document recovered from the municipal building in Prijedor during the search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same objection as previously outlined for the last exhibit, Your Honour, relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following the general policy, admitted into evidence as S133 A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've seen the establishment of the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. In October of 1991, did the Serbs leave the republic assembly and set up their own assembly of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In November of 1991, was a so-called referendum held of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: A plebiscite of the Serbian people was held, which is a form of expressing public opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result, was there a declaration of the Serbian republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that, then -- was there then an assembly of the Serbian people that dealt with the setting up of Serbian municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to have a look at, please, the records of the assembly of the 11th of December, 1991, which is document with the 65 ter number 37.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's the third document on the list, so it should be on the top of the bundle, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sejmenovic, obviously you didn't attend this assembly -- I see Mr. Ostojic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, this is the example. And I'm glad that counsel started by asking whether or not he attended. I think before the document is given to the witness and I think for him to evaluate or opine as to what may have occurred, perhaps some foundation questions such as whether he was in attendance, where he was during that time, before he is given an opportunity -- I'm sure other experts that they have already identified can give us testimony in connection with this document, but this the example that we previously -- or this is an example as to our previous motion on allowing a fact witness to give testimony on matters that are outside his scope and, respectfully for the witness, outside his competence since he was not present and has not been identified as an expert in this case or any others for that matter. So I would ask and insist that the Prosecutor lay some foundation before the witness as he is doing now obviously reading the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We look forward to the first introductory questions by the OTP, and then we'll come back to this probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, as I was saying, obviously you didn't attend this assembly. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I was not present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as we're going to see, did you personally know many of the people who spoke at this assembly; for example, Mr. Krajisnik, the president?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, because we spent a lot of time together in the parliament of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see the direct results in Prijedor of what was discussed and voted upon in this assembly, namely, the establishment of separate Serb municipal assemblies?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in Prijedor is almost an accurate reflection of what happened at the level of the republic. A Serbian assembly was in Prijedor as well outside the legal institutions of the local government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are the foundational questions I wish to ask. May I ask the witness to refer to the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is the understanding that the witness shall give testimony whether or not a decision, he didn't participate in the meeting, was echoed by the facts the witness was aware at that time in Prijedor and other areas. Is this the understanding?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour further, it deals with the issue of regionalisation with which the witness has already told us he is very familiar because it had been raised during the time that the assembly was a multiethnic one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course, for the Defence, the Defence may understand that it's not a jury here. It's professional Judges, and we know very well how to distinguish what is fact and what is opinion. I don't think it's unfair to introduce this document through the witness. We have to draw our own conclusions, as we did in the past. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, we can see that this is the transcript of the third session of the assembly of the Serbian people dated the 11th of December, 1991. It was opened by Krajisnik, who was the president of the assembly. And if we look at the agenda, Item Number 1 is the proposed recommendation to the armed forces on the preservation on the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. And if you could read, please, for the purposes of reading it into the transcript for the interpretation, rather, Item Number 2.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Item Number 2 reads as follows: "Proposed recommendation Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. (Decision) on the establishment of Municipal Assemblies of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then could you go, and I'm afraid I can't help you with the B/C/S, to page 9 -- I'm sorry, it's on page 9 of the translation at the bottom. And it's Item Number 2. There was a discussion about the army. Item Number 2, which reads "Proposed recommendation on the establishment of Municipal Assemblies." Have you found that, Mr. Sejmenovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Proposed recommendation (Decision) on the establishment of municipal assemblies of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then it says: "Dr. Milanovic, please read the proposed recommendation." Did you know who Dr. Milanovic was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who Dr. Milanovic is, but I assume, if he's the one reading the recommendation, then he must be one of the officials there. But it is also possible that he's one of the deputies. But I don't recognise the family name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I just want you, please, to read out what Dr. Milanovic said, the recommendation on the establishment of Municipal Assemblies of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The recommendation reads as follows: "Groups of deputies of the Serbian democratic party in Municipal Assemblies in Bosnia and Herzegovina in which the Serbian democratic party does not have the majority of the seats are recommended to pass decisions on the establishment of Municipal Assemblies of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we, then, move on, please, to the next -- it's our page 11 in the translation, to Dr. Karadzic's speech. And I don't think I need trouble to ask you whether you knew Mr. Karadzic. If we look, please, at page 12 of the translation, it's the paragraph I'd like you to read, Mr. Sejmenovic, of Dr. Karadzic's speech. It begins in English "In connection with these municipalities..."

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I've just found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just read, please, that paragraph until the words "their national economic and other rights."

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "In connection with these municipalities, the fact is that the Serbs are nevertheless maintaining a balance in some municipalities even though they are a minority and sometimes just about there and managing to protect primarily the human and civil rights as well as their national, economic, and other rights."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then could you go to the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then could you go to the paragraph "In some municipalities, it is really necessary..." and then I want to ask you a question about this. Just read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: All right. "In some municipalities, it really is necessary to create separate municipalities. I do not mean like Jewish ones which would be in charge of some affairs only, but it will be truly necessary for some cities to be border cities, that is, for some cities to have dual municipal authority."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, had you heard Dr. Karadzic or other members of the SDS expressing sentiments like this before?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. They tried to put forward such opinions in a milder form admittedly while we discussed these issues together in the Bosnia and Herzegovina parliament. Later on, they started to put forward the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina according to the ethnic principle in interparty negotiations, not only the territorial division, but also the division of its institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It talks about municipalities where Serbs were a minority. Were there municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina where the Muslim population were a minority?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had the SDA ever suggested that there should be, as it were, dual assemblies where they were in a minority?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. We continually fought this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move from Dr. Karadzic's speech to a speech made by Nenad Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's at page 13 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask whether you knew this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can read the first couple of sentences, and if you could then read the next paragraph. He said: "I'm in favour, and some perhaps remember that I insisted on Serb municipalities. But we have not finished the process we started, that of regionalisation." Now, could you read the next paragraph, please, so it can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The following paragraph reads as follows: "I think, I think that the order of moves should be planned. Plainly speaking, to break up the existing municipalities where the Serbs are not a majority for there are situations of some adjacent local communities of settlements belonging to two municipalities where Serbs are not a majority. This means that from two or three neighbouring municipalities, we have space to form a large, nice Serb municipality."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you heard this type of expression of sentiment said before? In other words, the breakup of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. At least, not in as many words as here. The need was discussed to introduce changes, to introduce borders, but no one was talking about such rough methods as breaking up, at least not openly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to look finally at the decision that was actually taken. Could you go, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For Your Honours, it's page 18 of the translation. And I'm not sure where it is in the Bosnian version, but it's headed "decision on the establishment of the assembly of the Serbian people in the municipality of..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 26. 26 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there we see the -- it was really the draft that was drawn up, I think. And can you just read, please, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph reads as follows: "The assembly of the Serbian people in the municipality of blank is hereby established as the highest representative organ and organ of power of the Serbian people in blank municipality".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then thereafter, we see --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Thereafter the text reads as follows: "The assembly of the Serbian people in the municipality shall be composed of representatives of the Serbian democratic party" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do it in a way that we can read it from the transcript, after the municipality of, there is a blank space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can summarise that Mr. Sejmenovic, because I want you to look at something said later by Mr. Kupresanin. Article 2 said that "The assembly would be composed representatives of the SDS who were in the municipal assembly as well as other representatives of Serb nationality." Then 3, "The Serbian people shall consider and decide issues related to the equality of the Serbian people." And I think we can leave out the remaining ones. Now, there was some further speeches on this draft. And could you look, please, now, at page 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The speech made by Vojo Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Is this after the form?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's after the form. If you go on, you will see there's a speech --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
