At the same time, we asked also Arsic, the commander of the 5th Brigade, and Zeljaja, the commander of the garrison, as well as Simo Miskovic, the president of the SDS, to set up joint patrols consisting of all the different ethnic groups in all endangered areas where people felt fear. These patrols were to be -- were to consist of neighbours or some mixed units, units the composition of which would inspire confidence and eliminate fear. But no such proposal ever came to anything. At the local level, at one point we did succeed in reaching an agreement because we put forward some arguments that could not be contested. We did not impose any conditions, but we just said that fear was felt on both sides and that people should join forces in defending their own households. In a number of places, we managed to put together neighbourhood guards, but then the SDS practically instructed the Serbs to pull out of these guards. And one day, they just pulled out without any explanation. They said that there was no need for those, that everyone should look after themselves, so this effectively put an end to our initiative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So by the local level, you mean what?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the local government units, the villages, the hamlets, places with mixed population, or where Muslim villages and Serb villages border on one another. So we asked for people to reach an agreement as those were people who had known each other for their whole lives to spend part of a particular night on guard duty together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two other matters on this: First of all, you said that you asked Arsic, Zeljaja, and Miskovic about these joint patrols. Why was it necessary to go to Miskovic as well as the army?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It was necessary to see him, too, because they, in a manner of speaking, worked as one team. They wielded force in their hands, and the others supported them. And in their turn, threatened with their own power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be obvious, but I'd still like you to spell it out. Who is "they" in this context who were working as one team?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: One of the teams was the head of the SDS, the commander of the 5th Kozara Brigade, and the commander of the garrison, so the military leadership and the political leadership, that is, the SDS leadership, working in unison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second thing is, I want to ask about this, you said you wanted to organise through the TO. What weaponry was available to the non-Serb TO units, or the TO units generally first of all?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The TO only had part of the weapons that rightfully belonged to it. Because the JNA had seized most of the weapons prior to the events we are now speaking about. What remained consisted mainly of old weapons, outdated weapons, mostly M-48 rifles or semi-automatic rifles, maybe a rifle or two that was sort of up to date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we come to the actual events directly leading to the takeover, what was the propaganda like, or the news that was coming out over radio and television in the period between February and April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The news were formulated in such a way that they had to be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. perceived as warmongering. They spoke about renewed threats to the Serbs and how there was a genocide underway against the Serbs for yet another time after 1941. They said the Serbs were to be prepared to defend themselves, that paramilitary units had to be set up -- were being set up to attack the Serbian people and the JNA. So typical war vocabulary that had been heard in the months preceding these events in a number of different areas. There was no way to avoid this. We could not use the TV repeater. And the local newspapers were staffed mostly by SDS members, at least in all the leading positions. So there was no way to counter this propaganda effectively and it certainly did have a major effect on the entire population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, let's deal with the Bosnian Serbs. What effect was all of this having on them from your contacts with ordinary Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of my personal contacts, so I'm talking about my friends, acquaintances, and people whom I was in touch with, I could monitor the spreading of these influences and effects through occasional conversations. I remember, for example, that when the army issued the mobilisation callup, a major number of Serbs were against it. And now I'm referring to the people that I talked to. As time passed by, an increasingly small number of Serbs was against the mobilisation. Eventually, there was a unanimous consensus that it was a patriotic thing to do to go to Croatia and defend Serbs. It was the same with threats to the Serbian people. It all became irrational at a certain point, so arguments were superfluous. The Serbian population was ready to fight, ready to take up arms. They did not really need an excuse to come from the neighbouring villages because propaganda had done its work by then. And a very important aspect of this propaganda was to show to the Serbian population that the greatest part of Prijedor was actually Serbian, and that Prijedor was a Serbian town. The census and the referendum, all the results, had been falsified to show that Prijedor was predominantly Serb in the past, who then became Yugoslavs. So there was constant propaganda to raise, in a manner of speaking, the awareness of the Serbian people, and eventually it did yield results. Most of them supported these activities, and then became passive onlookers as the atrocities began to take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effect was this type of propaganda having on the non-Serb populous in the Prijedor region?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It virtually paralysed the non-Serb population. We saw no way out of the situation. On one hand, there were the events taking place in Croatia, the Croatian border was there behind which a new Serb state had been established. Then we had the region of Banja Luka which had practically become independent, and they had its own military there in the town itself we had the 5th Kozara Brigade which already started referring to us as "the enemy." We could only rely on the news that we listened coming from the outside world, and the institutions that still existed, or parts thereof. We were trying to find the best possible solution, the most intelligent solution to get out of that situation, not to give them any pretext for any actions for the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people leave the Prijedor region as a result of what was happening before the takeover in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: There were no major departures of population from Prijedor before the takeover.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally this: On the propaganda, who were the most vocal in Prijedor about the genocide being planned against the Serbs and the like?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The local newspaper, Kozarski Vjesnik, wrote a lot about it. Sometimes, at the meetings that we held, the issue was discussed a lot by late Mr. Kovacevic, by Mr. Slobodan Kuruzovic. They appeared at these meetings as peacemakers. They were telling us how they had remained orphans after the Second World War, and that they knew what the war is and that they had seen concentration camps in the past, that they knew what it all meant. I remember two such discussions taking place at one of -- at some of the meetings. I was not quite clear about the reasons why Kovacevic and Kuruzovic were mentioning Jasenovac to us, as if we were the enemy threatening them. There was absolutely no reason whatsoever for such arguments. On several occasions, they appealed to us. They said that the entire leadership of the SDA should come with them to the battlefield in Croatia, that we should board a bus for Croatia with them so that they could show us on the spot what kind of destruction is engendered by war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's what Kovacevic and Kuruzovic were saying. Who was the most virulently, the strongest in speaking about the non-Serbs and what they had planned for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to single out individual cases. I know that several articles were published to that effect by Kozarski Vjesnik where Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it was said explicitly that a genocide was being prepared for the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any links between the SDS and Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were. There were journalists there who openly supported the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to come now to the events of the 29th, 30th of April of 1992. Before the takeover, did you notice anything about what your Serb neighbours were doing, particularly at night?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This was observed at several locations, not on the 29th or the 30th. It had already been observed ten days earlier on at least two occasions. What happened was that some of the residents left their homes, together with their wives and children. They even took property in their vehicles as they were leaving in several of these villages. Mostly, in villages bordering on non-Serb villages. One such case happened in my neighbourhood on two occasions. We never received any explanation for that. It was a kind of taboo. Nobody wanted to speak about it. They simply denied that it was happening, despite the fact that it was obvious to all of us in the town of Prijedor. If I remember correctly, this happened in the neighbourhood of Pecani and in some other areas, but I'm not sure about that. As for these other cases that I mentioned, I am quite certain, because I could personally observe that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when did you -- I'm sorry. How did you become aware of the takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The takeover of power occurred during the night, on the 30th of April. The next day, unaware of what had happened, I went to Prijedor by bus, as I had been doing every day. I went to the seat of my political party and the municipal building where I was supposed to carry out my daily duties and responsibilities. Some 200 metres away from the entrance to a Serb village, I noticed a police checkpoint. 1 kilometre after that, I noticed a military bus, and a military vehicle, and all passengers on the bus were required to show their ID. There were several such checkpoints manned by the military. And at all major locations inside the town itself, there were machine-gun nests, and one could observe that the presence of the police was increased. So when I got off the bus, I realised that the town was under occupation, but I did not have any specific information to that effect. I went to the premises of my party to see what it was all about, and after that I went to the town hall to, the municipality building, outside which I saw our officials, our deputies, who were denied access to the building. I also saw a Serbian flag hoisted at the flag pole outside the municipality building, and it was clear to me what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how did you find out the exact details of what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: When I went to the seat of my party, I found a number of officials there from the municipality and the police who had been denied access to their workplaces. So they came to the seat of the party to explain what was happening at their work and to see what should be done next. So it was at the party headquarters that we could obtain most of the information. At the same time, we listened to various jingles being played over the radio. There was talk about the liberation of the Serbian people, many nationalistic songs were being played.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever hear Dr. Stakic on the radio at this period?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember hearing him. I did listen to the radio on several occasions and heard a number of announcements, but I couldn't specifically state whether this was Stakic or someone else, or when Stakic was speaking and when it was someone else. I was listening to the contents of what was being said, not to the actual speaker because I knew what was at stake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even if you can't remember who, did members of the SDS appear on the radio to explain what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The announcements that we heard over the radio were made by the Crisis Staff. They said that they had finally lifted the blockade on the work of the government in Prijedor, that the institutions were finally functioning normally, that the population should go on as living and working as usual, as normal, that the extremists would be punished and sanctioned, and that they were -- and that they would ensure lasting peace in Prijedor. That was the essence of their announcements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us earlier that there was a formal announcement of the Crisis Staff's existence. Was that the first time you heard formally of the Crisis Staff existence?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first time that I heard a public announcement of the Crisis Staff, a public recognition of the fact that the Crisis Staff had taken over power in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we deal with, then, the various institutions after this takeover. What happened in respect of the police?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: At the party headquarters, we found out from the police officers who were not allowed to come to work, and from Mr. Talundzic, who was the chief of police at the time, that during the night, non-Serb police officers had been disarmed, that they were sent home from work, and that the next day, they were denied access to the police building. So it was no longer possible for them to enter the police premises, but were not given any specific explanation as to why they were being sent home. One of them was told that it was a very brief action which was supposed to finish within the next few days, that everything would return to normal after that. However, after 10 or 15 days, things turned out to be quite different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So thereafter, was the police force composed of anything -- of any other ethnicity than Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. The police force was composed of Serbs. There were publicly made appeals that all officials who were prepared to sign the pledge of loyalty to the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina would not lose their jobs. But this was done only nominally. This was not actually true. Practically speaking, there were no such cases. None of them were able to -- was able to keep their jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the Municipal Assembly, as it were, the members who were not Serbian, or the assembly itself really? Did that function at all?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: They could no longer enter the building, the municipal building. The president of the municipality, Muhamed Cehajic, was banned from the municipal building and was sent home. So he no longer appeared in this building. He never came back. Some lower-ranking officials were also Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sent home, and within the next few days, we learned that their employment in several cases had been officially terminated for reasons of absence from work or some alleged violations. So formal dismissals in respect of these people soon followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that that morning, you had gone into Prijedor to go to work. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what job were you actually doing at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I was an SDA official. I was the vice-president of the SDA. And by virtue of that capacity, I was often present in the municipality. I was also a member of the republican parliament, and I was often present -- I often went to some municipal bodies in order to be debriefed. So it was my obligation to go to these two addresses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever able after the 30th of April, 1st of May really, to get back into the municipal building to carry out your job there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. Only Serbs could enter the municipal building after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's slightly early. I know Your Honour said 4.15, but may I stop here. I'm going to go on to what happened after the coup. May I ask Your Honour whether Your Honour could perhaps consider overnight whether the first session on Monday afternoon could be taken up with reading documents. If it's not possible, I will have to try and make alternative arrangements with the other Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's come back to this issue tomorrow. And also, we all expect the reaction of the -- from the side of the OTP as regards a meeting of the parties, to put it neutral.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've taken instructions, and I'm awaiting -- the Prosecutor asked for time to consider the matter. So I'm awaiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Will it be possible until tomorrow evening?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that should be possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any observations by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Not at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, then we have to call it a day for today and resume tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
